summary: Defines ManageSieve, a protocol for securely managing Sieve email filtering scripts on a remote server. Users often cannot log into mail servers, so this lets them keep several scripts and be warned about scripts with syntax errors. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ManageSieve gives users a network protocol for managing the Sieve rules that filter incoming email. A client can validate and upload scripts, keep several versions on the server, and choose which one runs, while using TLS and SASL to protect access.

subtitle: Lets a client securely upload, check, and activate Sieve scripts on a mail server.

tldr.problem: Users need to manage mail-filtering scripts on servers that do not allow them to log in directly.
tldr.mechanism: ManageSieve defines a line-based client-server protocol for authentication, script checks, uploads, downloads, listing, renaming, deletion, and activation, with TLS and SASL security options.
tldr.outcome: Clients can manage multiple server-side scripts and see syntax errors before a script is stored or activated. RFC 5804 is updated by RFCs 7817 and 8553.

today: RFC 5804 is a Proposed Standard for ManageSieve. It is updated by RFC 7817 and RFC 8553.

sections.title: Managing Scripts Remotely
sections.content:
Sieve scripts filter incoming email, but users may not be able to log in to the server that stores their mail. ManageSieve supplies a client-server connection for managing those scripts remotely.

The server sends a greeting and capabilities, then accepts line-based commands and returns status results. Each command receives an OK, NO, or BYE response, with optional machine-readable detail.
sections.plainLanguage: ManageSieve lets an email user manage filtering scripts through a remote client. The server advertises what it supports and reports whether each requested action succeeded.

sections.title: Authentication and Transport Security
sections.content:
A client authenticates with the AUTHENTICATE command and a SASL mechanism. The server can advertise STARTTLS; after TLS starts, it sends its capabilities again so a client can detect changes.

Clients using SASL PLAIN over TLS must verify the server identity before sending credentials. The protocol requires implementations to support SCRAM-SHA-1 and PLAIN over TLS, and warns that unprotected sessions can be observed or changed in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication identifies the user who can manage scripts. TLS protects the connection, and a client must verify the server before using the PLAIN mechanism over TLS.

sections.title: Script Management Commands
sections.content:
LISTSCRIPTS shows stored scripts and marks the active one. GETSCRIPT downloads a script, PUTSCRIPT uploads one, RENAMESCRIPT changes its name, and DELETESCRIPT removes it.

SETACTIVE selects the script used for incoming mail; an empty name disables script processing. The server checks an uploaded script's syntax and supported extensions, and it must not store a script that fails validation.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands let a client list, retrieve, upload, rename, and delete scripts. Uploading does not normally activate a script; the client uses SETACTIVE to choose the one that filters new mail.

sections.title: Quotas and Script Checks
sections.content:
HAVESPACE asks whether a named script of a given size fits the user's quota. An affirmative reply is not a guarantee that a later upload will succeed because server storage can change.

CHECKSCRIPT asks the server to check a script without storing it. Servers must report syntax errors in a readable response and may report warnings for scripts that parse but may not do what the author intended.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can check space and script validity before uploading. The server still performs its own validation when a script is uploaded, and available storage may change after a space check.

sections.title: Protecting Scripts and Credentials
sections.content:
Without TLS, a SASL security layer, or another protection mechanism, ManageSieve traffic can be read or altered in transit. Implementations that support password mechanisms vulnerable to eavesdropping must provide a configuration that prevents their use without external protection.

Script names and contents can reveal private details about a user's mail setup. The protocol uses authentication and server-identity checks to protect script access, but deployments must configure those protections appropriately.
sections.plainLanguage: Scripts and credentials should travel over a protected connection. Without transport or SASL protection, another party may read or change the management conversation.
